title: Implementing a unified solver for nonlinearly constrained optimization
contribution: Describes SQP and interior-point (Lagrange-Newton) methods as combinations of eight building blocks in four layers and implements them in Uno, a modular C++ solver whose filtersqp and ipopt presets imitate filterSQP and IPOPT on 429 small CUTE problems (arXiv v2 read).
problem_entry: Entry through software redundancy: SQP and IPM solvers share components but are built as monolithic codes; four aims: hierarchy of strategies, comparison per instance, test bed, lower maintenance cost (abstract p. 1; pp. 2-3).
key_idea: Abstract inner/outer loop over eight ingredients (constraint relaxation, inequality handling, Hessian model, inertia correction, subproblem solver, globalization strategy, globalization mechanism) with progress measures generated by the reformulations; existing solvers become presets in a Cartesian product of strategies (pp. 5-7, 14-17).
assumptions: Nonconvex f, c; Fritz John Lagrangian with objective multiplier pi; combinations meaningful only under sufficient decrease and asymptotically equivalent reformulations; not all combinations converge; IPM + trust region prohibited (pp. 2, 4, 15, 17).
proof_devices: n/a: no theorems; convergence theory cited (filter SQP, line-search filter, l1 exactness) (pp. 10, 19)
Common notation of three progress measures (eta, omega_pi, xi) and predicted reductions expresses merit functions and filters as two acceptance rules (pp. 7-9)
Termination as outcome taxonomy: feasible KKT, feasible Fritz John (CQ fails), infeasible stationary, small trust region, loose tolerance over consecutive iterations (pp. 18-19)
experiments: 429 small CUTE problems in AMPL; baselines with versions (filterSQP 20010817, IPOPT 3.14.20/MA57, SNOPT, MINOS, LANCELOT, LOQO, CONOPT); unit objective evaluations; performance profiles; shifted geometric mean s=10 with failure=1e6 (filtersqp 18.08 vs filterSQP 18.73; ipopt 48.45 vs IPOPT 34.63); 12 ipopt-preset failures attributed to omitted features; logs public; no CPU time, no large problems (pp. 21-24).
positioning: Continuity, not criticism: fifteen solvers classified along the framework's axes in Table 6, revealing XSLP's missing globalization; follows Nocedal-Wright and Byrd-Curtis-Nocedal; cites own filter line with Waechter-Biegler (pp. 10-14, 35).
writing: Framework-plus-software contribution; colour-coded wheel of strategies and multicolour pseudocode; moderate hedging ('We believe ... potential'); abstract 'highly competitive' vs body 'perform well' (pp. 1, 3, 6, 19, 23, 24).
limits_future: Arbitrary combinations may not converge; ipopt preset weaker than IPOPT; small problems and evaluation counts only; filter flushed when mu changes; future quasi-Newton, MINRES, SLP-EQP, Sl1QP, parallel line search, TRS interface (pp. 15, 21, 23-24).

title: A globally convergent method for computing B-stationary points of mathematical programs with equilibrium constraints
contribution: MPECopt, a two-phase active-set method that solves a finite sequence of LPECs (as MILPs, often a single LP) and branch NLPs, proven under MPEC-MFCQ to reach a certified B-stationary point, and shown more robust and faster than regularization, penalty, plain-NLP and big-M MINLP (Bonmin) approaches on MacMPEC and a new large synthetic benchmark (arXiv v5 read).
problem_entry: Gap between computed and necessary stationarity: NLP form of MPECs degenerate (MFCQ fails everywhere), weaker stationarity concepts admit descent directions, active-set methods need MPEC-LICQ, LPEC methods are complex to implement (pp. 2-4, 9).
key_idea: Phase I: Scholtes regularization plus an LPEC at a near-feasible point whose any feasible point predicts a feasible BNLP; Phase II: trust-region LPEC at feasible iterate picks a BNLP, accepted only on objective decrease; LPEC steps never update iterates; LPEC solved as trust-region-bounded big-M MILP, solved to optimality only for the final certificate (pp. 4, 10-16, 20-22).
assumptions: f, c twice continuously differentiable; compact feasible set (Ass. 4.1); MPEC-MFCQ at every feasible point (Ass. 4.2; Example 3.1 shows MPEC-ACQ cannot be dropped); NLP solver returns stationary points with sufficient decrease or a feasibility stationary point (Ass. 4.3), worse-objective restoration case not treated; isolated BNLP stationary points for finite termination; exact BNLP solves (pp. 2, 11-12, 23-25, 30-31, 38).
proof_devices: Radius threshold rho-bar (16) equating reduced and full LPEC minimizers via Cauchy-Schwarz and branch exclusion (Lemma 3.1, p. 13; App. A p. 39)
Decomposition of the MPEC-linearized cone into BNLP linearized cones (41) and P(x+d) subset P(x) give BNLP feasibility (Lemma 3.2, p. 14; App. A pp. 39-40)
LP relaxation of the MILP equals the RNLP tangent-cone LP at S-stationary points, so certification costs one LP (Proposition 3.1, pp. 16-17)
Strict interior descent direction s(t)=s-bar+t*lambda*d under MFCQ, normalised with margin epsilon (Proposition 4.2, pp. 25-26)
Perturbation argument with rho interval (30) and ball inclusion B(x-tilde,rho) in B(x*,rho-bar) (Theorem 4.1, pp. 26-28); delta=sqrt(tau-bar) for Phase I (Corollary 4.1, p. 29)
Geometric trust-region shrinkage gives finite inner loop; cone scaling licenses early MILP termination (Proposition 4.3, Corollary 4.2, pp. 29-30)

Monotone bounded objective plus sufficient-decrease contradiction, following Chin-Fletcher and Fletcher-Leyffer-Toint case (C); finitely many BNLPs times isolated stationary points give finite termination (Theorem 4.2, pp. 30-31)
Two-variable worked examples with figures: Example 3.1 (MPEC-ACQ needed, pp. 11-12), 3.2 (trust region size and branch quality, pp. 13-14), 3.3 (tau too large predicts infeasible branch, pp. 19-20)
experiments: MacMPEC 191 problems and 75 synthetic MPECs (200-4000 complementarity pairs, up to 10000 variables, built to violate MPEC-LICQ, generator public); six methods; same IPOPT/MA27 options for all; success = B-stationary point, competitors checked post hoc (App. B) without charging the check; absolute and relative profiles; MacMPEC success 94.24% (MPECopt) vs 93.2/92.14/90.00/72.52%, MINLP 39 non-B-stationary stops; synthetic 96.16% vs 94.67%, NLP 16.00%; MILP node histograms exact vs early termination; App. C MILP LPEC solves up to two orders faster than regularization (pp. 32-41).
positioning: Surveys regularization/penalty, active-set and hybrid methods, criticising by assumptions (MPEC-LICQ) and stationarity strength; names implementation complexity as drawback of own LPEC methods [44, 46]; Remark 3.1 separates the method from MINLP using the Acta Numerica survey; credits Hu et al. and Jara-Moroni et al. for MILP view of LPECs (pp. 3-4, 17-18, 41).
writing: Contributions paragraph closes the introduction; each claim shown on a two-variable example with figure before proof; surprise markers ('Interestingly', 'Remarkably', 'Somewhat surprisingly'); results conclude 'competitive', conclusion 'generally faster and more reliable'; unexplained empirical regularity stated as open (pp. 4-5, 29, 35, 37-38, 41).
limits_future: Needs MPEC-MFCQ everywhere; restoration case untreated; exact BNLP solves; only B-stationary not global points even with convex MINLP relaxation; LPEC worst case exponential; HiGHS failed on two problems; future: inexact BNLP solves and explaining why regularization limits are B-stationary (pp. 15, 18, 23, 25, 38, 40).

quotes.text: Weaker stationarity notions exist, but most allow first-order descent directions, making them too weak as practical stopping criteria [46].
In summary, Algorithm 1 is not a MINLP algorithm; rather, it employs MILP solvers as a tool for solving LPECs.
